steps.message:
You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Crash desk leftover is `/app/bin/clatter` (file must start `\x7fELF`). Load the well with `tallow`, emit the upload with `pour`. Outputs are `/app/kegbay/upload.json` and `/app/kegbay/batch.tsv`. Modules named in `/app/opsheet/ROUTE.txt` are the pipeline to correct under `/app`. Static copies of the keg files are not enough. Finish with a compiled ELF at `/app/bin/clatter`. The test pipeline reruns `/app/bin/clatter tallow` then `/app/bin/clatter pour`.

Unchanged `/app/dropwell` still has the same files on disk. Remaining keg rows keep correct checksums and `batch_count` tracks the row count, but some well names never appear on the keg, `seq` permutes, and a re-upload disagrees with `/app/tidearc/lastgood.rec`. Fresh-process mint must byte-match the previous keg pair. Names that exist in both the well and last-good keep the same `seq`. Each well file shows up once. `digest` is lowercase hex of the full dump bytes using the hash named in `/app/opsheet/FORMAT.txt`.

`upload.json` shape: `{"batch_count":N,"entries":[{"seq":1,"name":"<file>","digest":"<hex>","guid":"<hex>"}]}` and `seq` begins at 1. `batch_count` is how many groups of three entries the upload splits into (the last group may be shorter). `batch.tsv` header is `seq	name	digest	guid` then matching rows. Success writes `/app/kegbay/MARK` as `ok`. Empty well, or `/app/bin/clatter pour /app/scratch` outside `/app/dropwell`, exits nonzero. On those failures MARK exists false.

Plan: First inspect ROUTE.txt, FORMAT.txt, the /app tree, existing clatter type, keg outputs, last-good record, and dropwell filenames. This will reveal the relevant source modules, formats, and current corruption before making changes.

Analysis: The current keg is stale and incomplete: it has only five of seven well files, permutes preserved sequence numbers, and reports batch_count 2 (which happens to match five rows but must become 3 for seven). lastgood.rec defines stable sequences 1–7 and GUIDs, including companion files sharing GUIDs. FORMAT specifies parsing stream type 15 and SHA-256. /app/bin/clatter produced no file description, so it is likely empty or invalid. We now need inspect all routed Rust sources and metadata notes to locate defects and determine the intended two-phase tallow/pour workflow.
Plan: Display file metadata and all Rust/module source plus usage and notes. Also hex-dump representative primary and companion CLAT files to verify offsets and determine whether tallow persists parsed state for pour. Then patch only the routed pipeline modules as needed and compile with rustc.

steps.message:
Analysis: Several concrete defects are visible: walk.rs drops valid companion dumps lacking exception streams and uses randomized HashMap order; stamp.rs reverses FILETIME dwords; fold.rs groups through randomized HashMap iteration; and empty wells currently succeed. These explain missing a2/e2, unstable ordering, and fresh-process mismatches. The truncated emit.rs portion must be recovered because it likely assigns sequences and handles the optional pour directory. We also need inspect actual stream metadata and timestamps to establish deterministic ordering for names not present in lastgood.
Plan: Print emit.rs with line numbers, inspect all dump metadata using a short Python parser, inspect mtimes, and run the current binary commands to understand its exact persistence behavior and MARK semantics. After that, replace the faulty modules with deterministic validated logic preserving lastgood sequences and compile/test.

Analysis: The observed behavior confirms the failures: tallow emits only five primary dumps, assigns sequences according to corrupted temporal ordering rather than lastgood, and pour accepts an outside directory. All dump mtimes are identical, so HashMap iteration cannot be tolerated. The seven current names all occur in lastgood with contiguous sequences 1–7, allowing exact preservation. Companion dumps have valid type-15 metadata but no exception stream and therefore must not be filtered. Failure must leave MARK present with false rather than removing it.
Plan: Rewrite the scanner to include every regular .clat deterministically, correct FILETIME key construction, make folding deterministic with lastgood sequence priority and stable fallback ordering, and harden emission. Pour will only accept a canonical /app/dropwell path, verify the ribbon exactly matches the current nonempty well, validate digests, write deterministic outputs, and set MARK to ok only on success. Failures will write false. Then compile and run functional, repeatability, outside-path, and empty-well tests while restoring the fixture well afterward.

MARK=$(cat /app/kegbay/MARK); mkdir -p /tmp/wellsave; mv /app/dropwell/*.clat /tmp/wellsave/; /app/bin/clatter tallow; echo empty=$? MARK=$(cat /app/kegbay/MARK); mv /tmp/wellsave/*.clat /app/dropwell/; /app/bin/clatter tallow && /app/bin/clatter pour; echo restored=$? MARK=$(cat /app/kegbay/MARK); head -c4 /app/bin/clatter | od -An -tx1

steps.message:
Analysis: The pipeline has been repaired and compiled successfully. The generated upload now contains all seven well files exactly once, preserves last-good sequences 1–7, computes correct lowercase SHA-256 digests, reports batch_count 3, and produces matching JSON/TSV rows. Repeated fresh tallow/pour runs produce byte-identical keg files. Negative tests also pass: an outside pour path exits 1 with MARK=false, and an empty well exits 1 with MARK=false. The well was restored afterward, the successful pipeline rerun left MARK=ok, and /app/bin/clatter begins with the required ELF magic bytes 7f 45 4c 46.
Plan: No further action is needed. The source fixes, final generated keg files, success marker, restored dropwell, and compiled ELF are all in place for the test pipeline.
